report:
## Evidence Summary

There is moderate, but nuanced, evidence supporting this claim.

**Meta-analytic evidence:** The strongest support comes from Kappelmann et al.'s systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials in chronic inflammatory conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease, etc.), where depression was measured as a secondary outcome. Across roughly 16 studies (with a subset of 7 RCTs specifically analyzed), anti-cytokine treatments produced a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms compared to placebo (Cohen's d ≈ 0.4), suggesting a potentially causal role for cytokines in depression (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/, https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167).

**Important caveat — population matters:** Evidence is much weaker when anti-cytokine drugs are tested directly in people with depression rather than inflammatory disease. Raison et al.'s RCT of the TNF-antagonist infliximab in *treatment-resistant depression* (without primary autoimmune disease) found no overall antidepressant benefit; benefit was confined to a subgroup with elevated baseline inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP >5 mg/L) (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1356541). A more recent 2024 proof-of-mechanism trial similarly targeted only depressed patients with high inflammation for TNF antagonism, reflecting the field's shift toward biomarker-stratified approaches (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-024-02751-x).

**Conclusion:** The claim is reasonably well-supported specifically for people with chronic inflammatory diseases who also have depressive symptoms — meta-analytic data show a moderate benefit. However, this doesn't establish that anti-cytokine drugs are broadly effective antidepressants; benefits appear concentrated in those with elevated inflammation, and results don't necessarily generalize to primary depression without inflammatory illness. The evidence is suggestive of a causal cytokine-depression link but not conclusive, given secondary-outcome measurement and heterogeneity across trials.
